process.title: Attacker impersonates [name]
process.desc: Another program or host pretends to be this service (for example with a stolen certificate, API key or a look-alike hostname), so clients and other services send it data or trust its responses. Typical controls: mutual TLS or signed service identities, short-lived credentials, certificate pinning for internal calls.

process.title: Internal endpoint accepts calls without authentication
process.desc: An internal API, message consumer or IPC channel trusts anything that can reach it, so any compromised process or container on the same network can send commands as if it were a legitimate caller. Typical controls: authenticate every caller (mTLS, signed tokens), network policies that limit who can connect.

process.title: Server-side request forgery (SSRF)
process.desc: The service fetches URLs or resources chosen by the user, so an attacker can make it call internal systems or cloud metadata endpoints on their behalf and act with the service's network position and identity. Typical controls: allow-list destinations, block internal and metadata addresses, separate egress proxy.

process.title: DNS spoofing redirects outgoing calls
process.desc: If name resolution can be poisoned or hijacked, the service connects to an attacker-controlled host instead of the intended one. Typical controls: verify server certificates on every outgoing connection, DNSSEC or trusted resolvers, avoid trusting hostnames alone.

process.title: Code or command injection through unvalidated input
process.desc: User-supplied data reaches an interpreter, template engine or system command, letting an attacker change what the service executes. Typical controls: strict input validation, parameterised APIs instead of string building, no shell calls with user data.

process.title: Binaries or libraries replaced on the host (DLL / path hijacking)
process.desc: Writable install or search paths let a local attacker swap in a malicious library or executable that the service then loads. Typical controls: read-only install directories, signed binaries, explicit library paths, least-privilege file permissions.

process.title: OS command injection via shell utilities
process.desc: User data is passed to shell tools without escaping, so characters like ; | or $( ) run extra commands with the service's permissions. Typical controls: avoid the shell, pass arguments as arrays, strict allow-lists for any value that reaches a command.

process.title: Malicious code in build or container supply chain
process.desc: Unpinned or unverified dependencies and base images let a compromised package or registry insert backdoors into what is deployed. Typical controls: pin versions and digests, verify signatures (e.g. Sigstore), private registry mirrors, SBOM and dependency scanning.

process.title: Security-relevant actions are not logged
process.desc: Changes to permissions, configuration or sensitive data happen without an audit record, so misuse cannot be detected or traced to a person. Typical controls: structured audit log (who, what, when, from where), forwarded to a store that the service cannot modify.

process.title: Log injection lets attackers forge or hide entries
process.desc: User input is written to logs unchanged, so newline or control characters can create fake entries or break log parsing. Typical controls: encode or escape user data in logs, structured (JSON) logging, protected central log storage.

process.title: Crashes leave no trace
process.desc: Unhandled errors terminate the process without logs, metrics or alerts, hiding attacks that crash the service on purpose. Typical controls: global error handlers, crash reporting, health checks and alerts on restarts.

process.title: Error messages reveal internal details
process.desc: Stack traces, SQL errors or configuration values are returned to the user, giving attackers file paths, versions and other details for further attacks. Typical controls: generic error responses, detailed errors only in server logs, disable debug mode in production.

process.title: Timing differences reveal secrets
process.desc: Comparing passwords, tokens or signatures with ordinary string comparison takes measurably different time, letting an attacker guess secrets byte by byte. Typical controls: constant-time comparison functions, rate limiting, vetted crypto libraries.

process.title: Data leaks between users or tenants through shared memory or caches
process.desc: Buffers, caches or pooled objects are reused without clearing, so one user's data can appear in another user's response. Typical controls: tenant-aware cache keys, clear buffers before reuse, isolation tests between tenants.

process.title: Secrets readable in memory dumps or swap
process.desc: Keys and tokens stay in memory in plaintext and end up in core dumps, swap or crash reports that others can read. Typical controls: disable or protect core dumps, keep secrets in a vault or HSM, minimise how long secrets stay in memory.

process.title: Resource exhaustion from unbounded requests
process.desc: Requests are processed without limits on size, rate or concurrency, so a burst of traffic ties up all threads, memory or connections. Typical controls: rate limits and quotas, request size limits, timeouts, bounded worker pools, autoscaling with caps.

process.title: Algorithmic complexity attacks (ReDoS, hash collisions)
process.desc: Specially crafted input makes a regular expression, parser or hash table do far more work than normal, pinning the CPU. Typical controls: safe regex engines or timeouts, input length limits, hardened parsers.

process.title: Message or task queue flooding
process.desc: Producers can enqueue unlimited work, so consumers fall behind, memory fills up and the service stops processing legitimate tasks. Typical controls: per-producer quotas, bounded queues with back-pressure, dead-letter queues and alerts.

process.title: Insecure deserialization runs attacker-controlled code
process.desc: Serialized objects from untrusted sources are turned back into objects without type checks, which can trigger code execution or bypass authorization. Typical controls: never deserialize untrusted native objects, use data-only formats (JSON) with schema validation.

process.title: Privilege escalation through environment or configuration of privileged helpers
process.desc: A privileged helper or setuid program trusts environment variables, paths or config files that a less-privileged user can change. Typical controls: sanitise the environment, absolute paths, drop privileges early, avoid setuid helpers.

process.title: Remote code execution through a vulnerable dependency
process.desc: A known vulnerability (CVE) in a library or framework lets attackers run code inside the service. Typical controls: dependency scanning, fast patching, minimal dependencies, runtime isolation (containers, seccomp).

datastore.title: Injection modifies stored data
datastore.desc: Unvalidated input reaches the database query or update logic, letting an attacker change records they should not be able to touch. Typical controls: parameterised queries, ORM field allow-lists, server-side validation of every write.

datastore.title: NoSQL query operator injection
datastore.desc: Objects or operators (such as $ne or $gt) supplied by the user are passed into NoSQL queries, bypassing filters or changing what is updated. Typical controls: accept only expected scalar types, strip operator keys, schema validation.

datastore.title: Backups or snapshots can be altered
datastore.desc: Backups, snapshots or replication streams can be modified without detection, so a restore brings back tampered data. Typical controls: write-once (immutable) backups, integrity checksums, restricted backup credentials.

datastore.title: SQL injection through filter or search parameters
datastore.desc: Search, sort or filter values are concatenated into SQL, letting an attacker read or change other data. Typical controls: parameterised queries, allow-lists for column and sort names, least-privilege database accounts.

datastore.title: Changes are not attributed to a user
datastore.desc: Records are created or modified without storing who made the change, so disputed or malicious changes cannot be traced. Typical controls: store the authenticated user and time on every change, database audit logging.

datastore.title: Historical records can be rewritten
datastore.desc: Audit or transaction records can be updated or deleted, so someone with write access can erase evidence. Typical controls: append-only tables or ledgers, write-once storage, separate audit database.

datastore.title: Administrators can delete logs without alerting anyone
datastore.desc: Privileged accounts can purge audit or event tables without the action being reported elsewhere. Typical controls: stream audit events to a SIEM in real time, alert on log deletion, separation of duties.

datastore.title: Bulk data extraction
datastore.desc: Missing per-record authorization or result limits lets a user or attacker page through and download far more data than they should. Typical controls: object-level authorization checks, result limits, anomaly detection on large reads.

datastore.title: Unencrypted backups exposed in shared storage
datastore.desc: Database exports are written unencrypted to buckets or file shares that other teams or tenants can read. Typical controls: encrypt backups, private buckets with strict policies, regular access reviews.

datastore.title: Data copied to test or staging without protection
datastore.desc: Production data or snapshots are copied to less-protected environments, exposing it to people and systems without production access controls. Typical controls: masked or synthetic test data, same controls for any copy of production data.

datastore.title: Lock contention or long-running queries block the database
datastore.desc: Expensive or deliberately slow queries hold locks and connections, so normal requests time out. Typical controls: query timeouts, connection pool limits, read replicas, rate limits on expensive operations.

datastore.title: Unindexed or wildcard searches exhaust resources
datastore.desc: Leading-wildcard or regular-expression searches scan whole tables and consume memory and CPU. Typical controls: require indexed search fields, limit pattern search, dedicated search engine, query cost limits.

datastore.title: Storage filled by unbounded writes
datastore.desc: Clients can write unlimited data (large payloads, endless log entries), filling disks until the database stops. Typical controls: size limits and quotas, retention policies, disk usage alerts.

interactor.title: Session hijacking
interactor.desc: Session cookies or tokens are stolen (via XSS, insecure transport or a shared device) and reused to act as the user. Typical controls: HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite cookies, short session lifetimes, bind sessions to device signals, re-authentication for sensitive actions.

interactor.title: Credential stuffing and password guessing
interactor.desc: Attackers try leaked username/password lists or guess passwords at scale to log in as real users. Typical controls: MFA, rate limiting and lockout, breached-password checks, bot detection.

interactor.title: Malware on the user's device intercepts input
interactor.desc: A malicious browser extension or malware reads keystrokes or changes requests before they are encrypted, acting with the user's identity. Typical controls: transaction confirmation on a second channel, MFA for high-risk actions, device posture checks for managed devices.

interactor.title: Session fixation
interactor.desc: The login process keeps a session identifier that an attacker set beforehand, so after the victim logs in the attacker shares the authenticated session. Typical controls: issue a new session ID at login and privilege change, reject unknown session IDs.

interactor.title: Requests are not signed or bound to a verified identity
interactor.desc: Actions can be submitted without strong authentication, so a user can credibly deny having made them. Typical controls: strong authentication, signed requests or transaction confirmations for important actions, audit logs with user and device.

interactor.title: Shared accounts make actions unattributable
interactor.desc: Several people use the same account or device session, so it is impossible to tell who did what. Typical controls: personal accounts, no shared credentials, re-authentication for sensitive actions.

interactor.title: Sensitive data stored on the client
interactor.desc: Tokens or personal data are kept in browser storage, caches or files on the device, where other software or people can read them. Typical controls: keep sensitive data server-side, short-lived tokens, Cache-Control: no-store for sensitive responses.

interactor.title: Secrets exposed in client logs or developer tools
interactor.desc: Tokens, internal URLs or personal data are written to the browser console or client logs, where they can be copied or collected. Typical controls: strip debug logging from production builds, never log secrets.

interactor.title: Cross-site scripting (XSS) steals data or tokens
interactor.desc: Injected script runs in the user's browser and reads page data or tokens, or acts as the user. Typical controls: output encoding, Content-Security-Policy, HttpOnly cookies, framework auto-escaping.

infrastructure.title: Rogue device impersonates [name]
infrastructure.desc: A device spoofs this host's network identity (IP, MAC or hostname) to receive traffic or join the network as a trusted machine. Typical controls: 802.1X network access control, device certificates, monitoring for duplicate addresses.

infrastructure.title: Firmware or OS configuration changed by an attacker
infrastructure.desc: Exposed management ports or missing secure boot let an attacker modify firmware or system configuration and persist on the host. Typical controls: secure boot, restrict management interfaces, configuration baselines with drift detection.

infrastructure.title: Host logs are not forwarded to a central store
infrastructure.desc: Logs stay only on the host, so an attacker who gains control can delete them and changes go unnoticed. Typical controls: forward logs in real time to a central SIEM, alert when log forwarding stops.

infrastructure.title: Secrets stored in plaintext on the host
infrastructure.desc: Configuration files, scripts or backups contain passwords and keys in cleartext, readable by anyone with access to the disk. Typical controls: secrets manager, disk encryption, file permissions, secret scanning.

infrastructure.title: Noisy neighbours exhaust shared resources
infrastructure.desc: Other workloads on the same host or hypervisor consume CPU, memory or I/O, degrading or stopping this system. Typical controls: resource limits and reservations, workload isolation, capacity monitoring.

infrastructure.title: Unpatched services allow remote takeover
infrastructure.desc: Known vulnerabilities in the OS kernel or exposed daemons let attackers execute code remotely and gain administrator control. Typical controls: patch management, minimise exposed services, host hardening and vulnerability scanning.

flow.title: Data modified in transit (man-in-the-middle)
flow.desc: An attacker on the network path intercepts the connection and changes requests or responses. Typical controls: TLS with certificate validation everywhere, HSTS, mutual TLS between services.

flow.title: Unprotected connection allows injected traffic
flow.desc: Without transport encryption and integrity checks, an attacker on the path can inject or replay messages into the connection. Typical controls: TLS or IPsec for all traffic, message signing and replay protection for critical messages.

flow.title: Network routing hijacked (BGP or DNS)
flow.desc: Manipulated routing or name resolution sends traffic through attacker-controlled systems. Typical controls: TLS with strict certificate validation, RPKI and route monitoring for public prefixes, trusted DNS resolvers.

flow.title: Unencrypted traffic can be read on the network
flow.desc: Plaintext protocols expose credentials and data to anyone who can capture the traffic. Typical controls: encrypt every flow (TLS, SSH, IPsec), disable plaintext protocols and fallbacks.

flow.title: Recorded traffic can be decrypted later (no forward secrecy)
flow.desc: Weak TLS configuration (for example static RSA key exchange or long-lived session ticket keys) lets someone who later obtains a key decrypt previously recorded traffic. Typical controls: TLS 1.3 or ECDHE cipher suites, rotate session ticket keys, disable outdated protocol versions.

flow.title: Data exfiltration through DNS or other covert channels
flow.desc: A compromised system smuggles data out inside DNS queries or other allowed traffic, bypassing firewalls. Typical controls: restrict outbound DNS to internal resolvers, monitor for unusual query volumes and lengths, egress filtering.

flow.title: Bandwidth or connection flooding
flow.desc: High volumes of traffic saturate the link or the receiving gateway, blocking legitimate requests. Typical controls: DDoS protection, rate limiting at the edge, autoscaling with limits.

flow.title: Slow-request attacks (Slowloris)
flow.desc: Clients open many connections and send data very slowly, keeping server connection slots occupied. Typical controls: request header and body timeouts, connection limits per client, reverse proxy in front.

flow.title: Expensive TLS handshakes exhaust the server
flow.desc: Clients repeatedly start or renegotiate TLS handshakes, which cost far more CPU on the server than on the client. Typical controls: disable client-initiated renegotiation, TLS termination with handshake rate limits, session resumption.
